The hook

The best view in Washington comes with a bill the sky pays.

Every flight past Rainier burns jet fuel, and planes are one of the few things we still can't just plug in.

The challenge

Hydrogen is the lightest fuel and the hardest to carry.

Batteries are far too heavy for an airliner. Liquid hydrogen packs almost three times the energy of jet fuel per kilogram and burns into water, but it takes four times the space and has to stay at −253 °C.

So the real question isn't the fuel. It's the whole airplane, built around it.

Leeham News, Bjorn's Corner: hydrogen storage (2022)
What we designed around

Eight things a hydrogen plane can't get wrong.

SafetyLeaks, fire and crashes. Hydrogen escapes fast and burns invisibly, so detection and venting come first.
AffordabilityGreen hydrogen is still expensive, so every kilogram of weight and drag we cut matters.
EfficiencyMore energy per kilogram only helps if the tank and powertrain don't eat it back.
ClimateZero CO₂ in flight, but water vapor and contrails still warm the planet.
NoiseRegional airports sit next to neighborhoods, so quieter props are part of the deal.
End of lifeComposites that end up in landfills defeat the point. Ours have to come apart and be reused.
AccessSmall cities, not just hubs. It has to work at airports that don't have a hydrogen plant yet.
InfrastructureThe plane is useless without the fuel, the storage and the people to run it on the ground.
The solution

Meet Halcyon H2-50.

A 50-seat regional airliner that runs on liquid hydrogen through fuel cells, with an airframe borrowed from five animals.

Concept targets, not certified specs
Bio-inspired aerodynamics · 1

A nose from a kingfisher, a skin from a shark.

Japan reshaped its 500 Series bullet train around a kingfisher's beak and it ran about 10% faster on 15% less energy. Shark-skin riblet film already flies on 777s and cuts fuel burn by about 1%, and that adds up fast across a whole fleet.

Composite structures · the tank

A fuel tank colder than anywhere on Earth.

NASA and Boeing tested a 5.5 m all-composite cryogenic tank that came out 30% lighter and at least 25% cheaper. At −253 °C, metals get brittle, hydrogen sneaks through tiny cracks, and layers shrink at different rates. That's a materials problem first.

CompositesWorld (2014), NASA/Boeing composite cryotank test
Composite structures · the skin

A skin that bleeds and heals.

Like blood vessels, tiny channels inside the carbon fiber carry two liquids. When a crack breaks them open, the liquids mix and harden, healing at nearly 100% efficiency, again and again.

H. Zell, CC BY-SA 3.0

Inside the cabin, flax-fiber panels replace some glass fiber, so the parts nobody sees are grown, not mined.

RECRUIT AT UWSAMPE (composites)Material Advantage
Beckman Institute, Univ. of Illinois (2014): repeated self-healing in fiber composites · UW MSE clubs page
Mechanical · thermal management

The cold is a feature, not a problem.

The hydrogen has to warm up by about 300 °C before the fuel cells can use it, and the fuel cells make heat we have to dump. So we let one fix the other, and the water that comes out goes straight to the cabin tap.

Why mechanical: heat exchangers, pumps, valves and the tank's mounts all live where thermodynamics meets hardware. One cryogenic leak decides whether this plane ever flies.

RECRUIT AT UWASMEFormula MotorsportsBoeing Advanced Research Center
Sustainable manufacturing

Welded, not riveted. Melted down, not dumped.

Europe's thermoplastic fuselage demonstrator welds its stiffeners on instead of drilling thousands of holes. It came out about a tonne lighter than aluminum and skips the autoclave, cutting production time by up to 40%. Thermoplastics also re-melt, so scrap and old parts become new ones.

We'd build it next door. Robots like this fiber-placement head are made in Mukilteo, and UW's Boeing Advanced Research Center is already funded to automate thermoplastic parts.

DLR (2023) MFFD · UW A&A News (2019) BARC $1.2M Clean Energy Fund grant
Electroimpact, CC BY-SA 4.0
Electrical · the powertrain

Fuel cells, superconducting wires, quiet props.

Fuel cells turn hydrogen into electricity and water, with no flame. Then we use the −253 °C fuel one more time: it chills the cables and motors until they superconduct. Airbus expects that trick to at least halve the weight and electrical losses of the powertrain.

Electrical · sensing and software

A plane with a nervous system that dodges clouds.

Fiber-optic sensors woven into the composite feel strain, cold spots and leaks everywhere at once, and feed a digital twin of the airframe.

Hydrogen puts out about 2.6× more water vapor per unit of energy, but it may cut contrail ice crystals by 80 to 90%. Our flight software reads humidity forecasts and nudges the route around the air where contrails would linger.

Why ECE: power electronics, sensors, controls and code are what turn a tank of hydrogen into a plane that flies itself safely.

Atmos. Chem. Phys. 25, 7903 (2025), hydrogen contrail ice crystals
SounderBruce, CC BY-SA 4.0
Civil · the ground game

No plane flies without an airport that makes fuel.

We design the hydrogen hub: solar and electrolysis on airport land, a liquefier, an insulated tank farm with safe setbacks, and pipes to the gate. Smaller airports get swappable fuel pods by truck, an idea first flown at Moses Lake in 2023.

Washington is ready for it. The DOE picked the Pacific Northwest Hydrogen Hub for up to $1B, and more than 220 airports have joined Airbus's hydrogen hub study.

Why civil: siting, foundations, water supply, permits and safety zones are what turn a hydrogen idea into concrete on the ground.
